verses.translation_literal: YHWH has reigned! Let the earth be glad; let many coastlands rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is king. Let the whole earth break into gladness, and let the far shores answer, coast after distant coast, each one rejoicing.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the throne-shout of the psalms: the verb comes before its subject's weight is felt, so the cry is 'YHWH reigns!' with the name placed first, as an acclamation, the way a crowd would hail a new king in the ancient Near East. Everything after it is a call for the world to react. Nothing in the Hebrew says 'thereof': the KJV's closing 'be glad thereof' is an addition, and its 'multitude of isles' hides a plain word, 'many'.

The 'isles' (אִיִּים) are the coastlands of the Mediterranean, the edge of the known world for a landlocked highland people. Their gladness is the point: the king's reach goes to the farthest harbours. The two verbs of gladness (גִּיל, שָׂמַח) are standard pairs of festival joy.

philological_notes.note: A perfect verb used in the cry 'YHWH has become king / reigns'. Meiri takes the perfect as past standing for the future, as prophets often speak; others read it as the shout at a king's enthronement.
Coastlands and islands; Radak glosses it as the borders of the nations, and Metzudat David as the dwellers of the sea-islands. It means the far Mediterranean world.

verses.translation_literal: Cloud and thick darkness [are] around him; righteousness and justice [are] the foundation of his throne.
verses.translation_dramatic: Cloud wraps him, and a thick darkness beyond it, so that no eye can reach him. Yet under the throne itself, set firm as bedrock, lie righteousness and justice.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene recalls Sinai: the cloud and 'thick darkness' (עֲרָפֶל) are the covering of the God who appears and is not seen. The audience would hear the mountain, and the terror of Exodus. The KJV's 'Clouds and darkness' pluralizes עָנָן, which is singular in the Hebrew, and its plain 'darkness' loses the specific sense of עֲרָפֶל, 'thick darkness, dense cloud', the storm-gloom into which Moses went at Sinai. The KJV's 'habitation of his throne' also mistakes מָכוֹן, which means a fixed base, a foundation or established place, for a dwelling. The ASV 'foundation' is correct.

The contrast is the whole verse. Hiddenness, in Malbim's reading, means that providence is veiled, not absent. In the ancient world a throne's base was its legitimacy; a king who sat on injustice sat on sand. Here the base is moral, and it is not hidden.

philological_notes.note: Thick darkness, the heavy storm-gloom of Sinai theophanies; Metzudat Zion glosses it as the thickness of the cloud.
From the root 'to be firm, established': a fixed base or place. The KJV 'habitation' mistakes the sense. Ibn Ezra explains the phrase as 'for by righteousness the throne is established'.

verses.translation_literal: Fire before him goes, and it burns all around his foes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before him walks fire. It does not wait; it circles his enemies and closes, and everything standing against him is licked and consumed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm-god image, taken over from the surrounding peoples and given to YHWH alone: fire marches before him as a herald, as in the Canaanite pictures of Baal advancing with thunderbolts, and as in the Sinai fire. In Israel's poetry the fire does not belong to some lesser deity; it is his vanguard.

The KJV's 'burneth up' is a fair gloss, but the Hebrew verb וּתְלַהֵט is a flame-word, from the root of לַהַט, 'flame' (as in the flaming sword of Gen 3:24), and the unusual 'all around' (סָבִיב) closes the circle: Radak notes that there is then no place left to flee. 'Enemies' is צָרָיו, those who press him, the 'narrow-makers'.

philological_notes.note: To blaze or flame; Metzudat Zion links it to 'flaming fire' (Ps 104:4). Radak reads the encircling 'around' as leaving no place to escape the fire.

verses.translation_literal: His lightning flashes lit up the world; the earth saw and writhed.
verses.translation_dramatic: His lightning tears the sky and the whole world stands lit in white; the earth sees, and shudders like a woman in labour.
verses.directors_commentary:
The lightning is the visible face of the cloud-hidden king (v. 2): the dark is split, and what the nations could not see becomes plain for a heartbeat. The effect is sudden light followed by trembling. The KJV 'enlightened' is archaic and, to a modern ear, suggests teaching; the Hebrew says 'lit up' (הֵאִירוּ), physically. 'Trembled' also softens: the verb חוּל is used of birth pangs and of whirling or writhing (Rashi cites the birth sense), so the earth is convulsing, not just shivering.

תֵּבֵל, 'the world', is the inhabited, fruitful earth, while הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth', is the ground itself; both are the audience for the sight. Ibn Ezra notes the clever, who see, are the ones who tremble.

philological_notes.note: The inhabited, productive world, a poetic word often paired with 'earth' as here. It is not the bare ground.
To writhe, twist, be in labour; Rashi cites the labour-pain use ('pain like a woman in labour', Ps 48:7, Mic 4:9), Metzudat Zion links it to the word for trembling.

verses.translation_literal: Mountains like wax melted from before YHWH, from before the Lord of all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: The mountains, the oldest and hardest things in the world, run like wax in the heat, melting away from the face of the LORD, from the face of the Lord of the whole earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mountains were the seats of the gods in the ancient Near East: Baal on Zaphon, the high places of Canaan. For them to melt is a polemic: the supposed thrones of the gods run like a candle. A mountain-dweller's world was built on those peaks, so this is the collapse of the visible order.

The verse has a pair of parallel 'from before' lines (מִלִּפְנֵי), a repetition the KJV renders as 'at the presence', which is true to the sense but loses the face: the Hebrew says 'before his face'. The KJV's 'hills' softens הָרִים, which is 'mountains'. Wax (דּוֹנַג) was a household substance, beeswax for seals and lamps, which melted in a flame or a summer sun.

Radak and Metzudat David take the 'mountains' as a figure for the proud rulers; I keep them as mountains and leave the figurative reading to the commentary.

philological_notes.note: Beeswax, a common figure for melting; Rashi and Radak simply gloss it as 'wax'.
'Lord of all the earth': a title that challenges the claim of local gods and territorial lords. Malbim reads it as against a belief that each land had its own lord.

verses.translation_literal: The heavens declared his righteousness, and all the peoples saw his glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: The heavens speak, and what they proclaim is his justice. And every people looks up and sees it: his glory, laid open to all.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient world the heavens were crowded with gods; the sun, moon and stars were divine powers. Here they are only heralds, and what they announce is YHWH's righteousness. The nations, not just Israel, see it: the audience is universal.

On tense: הִגִּידוּ is a perfect and וְרָאוּ a waw + perfect, forms that can be read as past or as present. The YLT and ASV ('declared ... have seen') take the past, as the earth 'saw' in verse 4; the KJV takes the present ('declare ... see'). Both are possible, and I keep the literal 'declared ... saw' in the first layer and the present in the dramatic one. The KJV 'all the people' does make a singular of the plural הָעַמִּים, 'the peoples'. The reading of 'heavens' is disputed: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take them as those who live in heaven, the angels; the Targum agrees ('angels of the height').

philological_notes.note: To tell, make known, report. The Targum renders 'the angels of the height will tell', Ibn Ezra 'the dwellers of heaven'.
His righteousness; Meiri notes the word sometimes means 'kindness' (as in Israel's rescue), sometimes straight justice.

verses.translation_literal: Let them be ashamed, all servants of an image, those boasting in worthless things; bow down to him, all gods.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be shamed, every one who serves a carved figure, who made a boast of their nothings. And you, all you gods: bow down to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse that aims the whole psalm. The 'image' (פֶּסֶל) is the carved cult statue, the very thing around which the other peoples organized their worship, and 'worthless things' (אֱלִילִים) is the contemptuous word: it sounds like אֵל, 'god', but means 'nothings', a deliberate pun. The KJV's 'graven images' and 'idols' blurs the pun; its 'confounded' is archaic for 'put to shame'. In the ancient world a nation's gods were its security; to see them shamed was to see the nation shamed.

The last line has a famous question. 'All gods' (כָּל־אֱלֹהִים): the KJV 'ye gods' reads it as a command to deities. Radak and Metzudat David take them as the host of heaven, who bow before him; the Targum has 'all peoples', and Ibn Ezra notes that some read them as angels. The Hebrew verb is an imperative, though Radak and Meiri take it as past used for the future.

philological_notes.note: 'Worthless things', a contemptuous word for idols that resembles אֵל 'god' and אֱלֹהִים. The pun is deliberate: gods who are 'not-gods'.
Those who boast or praise themselves; Rashi 'those who glory in the service of idols', Metzudat David 'who praise themselves'.
'All gods': read as the host of heaven (Radak, Metzudat David, Meiri), or as all who serve other gods (Radak's alternative, the Targum 'all peoples').

verses.translation_literal: Zion heard and rejoiced, and the daughters of Judah were glad, because of your judgments, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Zion hears it, and rejoices; the daughters of Judah, in their towns, break into gladness because of your judgments, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera narrows from the world to a single hill. Zion, the city, 'heard' the news first and rejoices: the verbs change from the nations' terror to a home audience's relief. The speech turns, too: for the first time in the psalm, God is addressed directly ('your judgments').

'Daughters of Judah' is not a family: it is the villages around a city, the way a city's daughters are its dependent towns (Metzudat Zion cites Numbers 32:42, 'Kenath and her daughters'). The two verbs of joy, שָׂמַח and גִּיל, are the same pair as in verse 1, so the verse echoes the opening call and answers it. The KJV's 'because of thy judgments' hides that מִשְׁפָּטִים are acts of judging, verdicts carried out. Rashi glosses them simply as 'your vengeance'. Anyone who has lived under a conqueror would hear this as release.

philological_notes.note: The towns of Judah; Metzudat Zion compares 'Kenath and her daughters' (Numbers 32), Meiri 'the cities of Judah'.
Acts of judgment, verdicts enacted; Rashi glosses 'your vengeance'.

verses.translation_literal: For you, YHWH, [are] Most High over all the earth; exceedingly you are exalted over all gods.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you, O LORD, are the Most High over all the earth. You are raised far, far above every god there is.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for all the joy comes last, as a statement of rank. 'Most High' (עֶלְיוֹן) was an ancient title of the supreme God in Canaan; the psalm gives it to YHWH and denies it to every rival. The ancient reader knew that kingdoms and their gods were ranked by victory: when YHWH's judgments land, the ranking is displayed.

The KJV 'high above all the earth' renders the title as an adjective and loses it; the ASV 'most high' keeps it. The KJV's 'far above all gods' is right in sense: מְאֹד means 'exceedingly', 'very much'. Radak and Metzudat David read 'gods' here as the host of heaven worshipped until now; Malbim reads the exaltation as the difference between gods that must act by nature and a God who acts by will and justice.

philological_notes.note: 'Most High', an old title of the highest God, which the psalm applies to YHWH over the whole earth.
Niphal 'you are/have been raised'; Metzudat Zion links it to the root of going up and praise, Metzudat David glosses 'you are superior and praised above all gods'.

verses.translation_literal: Lovers of YHWH, hate evil! He guards the lives of his faithful ones; from the hand of the wicked he rescues them.
verses.translation_dramatic: You who love the LORD, hate evil. He keeps watch over the lives of those faithful to him, and out of the hand of the wicked he pulls them free.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns from the world to the listener: love of YHWH is not a mood but a stance, and here it is defined by what one hates. In the ancient Near East love was a covenant word, loyalty owed to a lord; to love YHWH is to be his loyal vassal, and loyalty has an enemy.

The KJV's 'saints' is a trap: חֲסִידִים are not canonized holy persons but 'the faithful', those who keep covenant loyalty (חֶסֶד). Likewise 'souls' (נַפְשׁוֹת) is 'lives' or 'persons', not an inner spirit. And 'the hand of the wicked' is the Hebrew idiom for their power, a grasp, not a literal fist. The 'rescuing' is the verb of pulling out from a trap or a river.

philological_notes.note: 'His faithful ones', those who practise covenant loyalty. The KJV 'saints' suggests canonised holiness; the sense is loyalty, not sanctity.
'Lives, persons': not a soul separable from the body. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David read the verse as protection of the person from enemies.

verses.translation_literal: Light is sown for the righteous, and for the upright of heart, joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: Light is sown like seed for the righteous, and for those whose hearts are straight, joy, waiting to rise.
verses.directors_commentary:
A farmer's image: light is not handed out but sown, like grain, and it will come up. For a farming people, sowing meant waiting through a dry season on trust that the field would answer. That is the promise made here: the gloom of verse 2 is a season, and the righteous are planted.

The KJV's 'gladness' is softer than 'joy', though שִׂמְחָה is the festival word. 'Upright in heart' is יִשְׁרֵי־לֵב, 'straight of heart', a literal picture of a heart that does not bend. The line has no verb for the second half ('for the upright... joy'), and the Hebrew sets the two lines side by side, as in Metzudat David's reading that joy too is sown. Rashi insists the sowing is real: it is prepared to sprout.

philological_notes.note: 'Is sown', passive of the sowing verb. Rashi: 'a real sowing, prepared to sprout for them'; Ibn Ezra: a little sown, much harvested. Meiri notes a suggestion that the word stands for 'shines' (זרוח), but I keep 'sown'.
'Straight of heart', whose inner intention is without crookedness.

verses.translation_literal: Rejoice, righteous ones, in YHWH, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rejoice, you righteous, in the LORD. And give thanks as you remember his holiness, the holy name that you call to mind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends with a command to the congregation, as a hymn ends in the liturgy: the choir is told to sing. 'Rejoice in YHWH' means that he is the sphere of the joy, not just its cause.

The last phrase is hard. 'Remembrance of his holiness' (זֵכֶר קָדְשׁוֹ) is the 'memorial' by which God is invoked, that is, his name: Radak says plainly 'it is his name', and Metzudat David 'the memory of his holy name'. The KJV 'at the remembrance of his holiness' keeps the Hebrew but leaves the reader unsure; the ASV 'holy memorial name' commits to the name reading; the BBE 'praising the memory of his holy name' does the same. The verb הוֹדוּ is 'give thanks / confess', a public act in the temple, not only a feeling.

philological_notes.note: The 'memorial' of his holiness: his name, by which he is called to mind in worship. Radak glosses 'his name'; Metzudat David 'the remembrance of his holy name'.
To give thanks, acknowledge publicly; it is the liturgical word for praise in the temple.
